title: Leaders Who Overshare
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Admired Leadership argues that transparency, though a genuine leadership virtue, has a harmful excess. The piece acknowledges that team members want to be included and to understand how their leader sees the work and the future. It then identifies distinct failure modes of oversharing: voicing doubts that erode confidence, announcing half-formed decisions that people start acting on, disclosing private personal matters that unsettle rather than connect, and flooding people with data and metrics they must then sort. The author pushes back on contemporary advice that leaders must always be vulnerable, insisting on clear boundaries. The closing image distinguishes a light from a floodlight: share what people need to perform and feel included, not everything.
points: Transparency about organizational health builds trust only up to a point; broadcasting a leader's own doubts undermines the team's confidence.
Sharing decisions before they are 'even partially baked' is dangerous because people respond and act on information as soon as it exists.
The piece explicitly challenges the fashionable advice to be vulnerable, arguing that over-disclosing personal matters unsettles people rather than deepening connection.
Information overload is itself a performance cost, forcing team members to sort relevant from irrelevant data and slowing their thinking.
quotes: Team members want to be included and privy to what is going on. They relish fast-breaking news and value understanding how the leader sees and makes judgments about the team, the future, and the work at hand.
Like everything else in life, too much of a good thing can become harmful. When leaders overshare or provide too much information, they can create havoc and dismay within the team.

Similarly, leaders who disclose decisions before they are even partially baked create nervousness and expectation. Once the information exists, people respond and act on it, many times to the detriment of team success.

Leaders who over-disclose personal information, including their most private peccadillos, don’t foster a deeper connection with others. They freak them out. Despite the contemporary advice that leaders need to be vulnerable, clear boundaries need to be set.

Giving people too much information, too much data, or too many metrics about the task at hand can overwhelm them. At a minimum, too much information will slow people down and gum up their ability to think things through. When confronted with too much data, team members must sort out what is relevant and what is not.

Good leaders rightly promote a transparent and open workplace. They should work hard to share the information people need to perform and feel included. But when they overshare, providing too much disclosure or information, they turn a positive into a negative.
